name: Custom chin implant (silicone/Medpor)

lead: A chin implant is a shaped piece of synthetic material, most often silicone or porous polyethylene (Medpor), placed through a cut under the chin or inside the lower lip to push the chin forward. It is a long-established cosmetic operation, often done alongside nose surgery.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a cheaper, reversible alternative to sliding genioplasty, with debate over whether it is enough for a very recessed chin and over custom (patient-specific) designs made from CT scans.

paras: The implant sits on the front of the jawbone and adds bulk, increasing projection and sometimes height or width. Silicone is smooth and removable; porous polyethylene allows tissue ingrowth and is harder to remove. Custom implants are designed from a scan of the individual's jaw.

Reported risks include swelling, hematoma, infection, implant displacement, bone changes under the implant, and nerve numbness. Surgical literature notes that complication rates depend on technique and surgeon experience. It is performed as an Rx surgical procedure by licensed surgeons.

lead: A chin implant is an alloplastic (synthetic) device placed over the lower border of the mandible to increase the projection, and sometimes the height or width, of the chin. Common materials are silicone, porous high-density polyethylene (often sold as Medpor), expanded polytetrafluoroethylene and, more recently, patient-specific implants made from materials such as PEEK. [1][2]

The operation is commonly performed together with rhinoplasty or a facelift. Surgical reviews describe a continuing debate over whether an implant or an osseous (bone-cutting) genioplasty is the better operation for a given patient, and state that complication avoidance depends on technique and surgeon experience. [3][1]

In looksmaxxing communities, chin implants are discussed as a lower-cost, less invasive option than sliding genioplasty, and the term 'custom implant' refers to a design made from the person's own CT scan. A small number of registered trials have compared patient-specific implants with computer-guided genioplasty. [4][2][5]
infobox: Under the chin or inside the lower lip
Removable, more difficult with porous materials

paras: Encyclopedic summaries list silicone as the most common material, noting it can be removed and can shift or be associated with bone resorption; porous polyethylene (Medpor), into which tissue grows and which is harder to remove; ePTFE, fixed with titanium screws; and donor-derived dermal grafts. [1]

Custom or patient-specific implants are designed from a CT scan and fabricated to the individual's anatomy. Registered trials have examined PEEK patient-specific implants for chin deficiency (microgenia). [2]

A review of complications in chin augmentation states that there has been much debate about whether implant placement or osseous genioplasty is superior. [3] An encyclopedia summary states that bone-based osteotomy usually gives a more dramatic correction than a prosthetic implant. [1]
On looksmax.org, users discuss the choice between implant and genioplasty, including cost, reversibility, and whether an implant can substitute for waiting for a bone-moving operation. [6][7]
Common effects are swelling, bruising and temporary numbness or lip weakness; less common risks include infection, implant displacement, bone changes, and nerve injury. [3][1]
A 1981 clinical analysis of alloplastic chin implants in the otolaryngology literature is one of the early published series examining the outcomes of implant mentoplasty. [8]

Forum threads include questions about whether a chin implant is 'enough' on its own, whether implants suit people with a recessed chin and short face, and requests for ratings of before-and-after photographs. [9][10][11]

Some users ask about vertical lengthening via an implant versus a genioplasty. [12] Others discuss fat grafting as an alternative to either option [13]; the surgical literature describes autologous fat grafting to the chin as an adjunct in facial rejuvenation. [14]

Published surgical literature on chin augmentation is mainly narrative reviews and case series. [3][8] A registered trial (NCT04817930, completed, 20 participants) compared a patient-specific alloplastic chin implant with computer-guided genioplasty, assessing soft-tissue results after one year. [4] Other registered trials have examined the accuracy of patient-specific PEEK implants and of patient-specific implants in genioplasty. [2][5]
